title: Biomass distribution and swarm characteristics of Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) in the Western Indian sector of the Southern Ocean
content:
Abstract
The Indo-Pacific region has recently been proposed as a potential climate refuge for Antarctic krill. Here, the biomass distribution and swarm characteristics of Antarctic krill are provided based on an acoustic-trawl survey conducted in the southwestern Indian Ocean (35–75°E) during the 2019/2020 austral summer. Using a swarm-based acoustic identification method, krill mean areal biomass density was estimated to be 7.47 g m⁻² with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 37.29% for the entire survey area. Krill spatial distribution showed strong heterogeneity, characterized with that >85% of the one nautical mile distance intervals exhibited krill densities <1 g m⁻² and ∼80% were absence of krill swarms. While no consistent spatial pattern was observed, swarms with higher-density (>100 g m⁻²) were more frequently observed along the 50°E and 60°E transects. Clustering analysis indicated that krill length–frequency distributions from trawl sampling generally fell into two groups, with one mainly composed of smaller-sized krill (<30 mm) and the other mainly composed of larger-sized krill. The smaller-sized krill tended to be widely distributed in the open sea of the survey area, while the larger-sized krill cluster (>30 mm) were more concentrated in waters close to nearshore and eastern area. Further comparative analysis indicated significant differences in swarm characteristics between the two size-based swarms: swarms composed of larger-sized krill were characterized by relatively greater depth, thicker vertical extent, and higher packing density than the swarms composed of smaller-sized krill. These findings improve our understanding of krill population dynamics and swarming behavior in the Western Indian sector of the Southern Ocean.
